_comment: Every scientific claim shown in the app must point to a source in this list by id. Each VERIFIED entry records its consultation date in 'accessed'. 'notes' are shown in the UI (English).

sources.title: About High Blood Pressure
sources.notes: Blood pressure categories (normal, elevated, stage 1, stage 2) and the >180 systolic and/or >120 diastolic severe-hypertension threshold.

sources.title: Pulse
sources.publisher: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine) / A.D.A.M. Medical Encyclopedia
sources.license: Copyrighted (A.D.A.M. Medical Encyclopedia via MedlinePlus); linking allowed, own paraphrase only
sources.notes: How to take a pulse (wrist, neck) and the adult resting range of 60 to 100 beats per minute.

sources.title: Low Blood Sugar (Hypoglycemia)
sources.notes: Low blood sugar is below 70 mg/dL; severe is below 54 mg/dL. The CDC treatment page cites 55 mg/dL for severe; this app uses 54 mg/dL from the definition page.

sources.title: Treatment of Low Blood Sugar (Hypoglycemia)
sources.notes: The 15-15 rule: 15 g of carbohydrate, wait 15 minutes, recheck. Severe low blood sugar needs glucagon and emergency care.

sources.title: Definitions of Signs, Symptoms, and Conditions of Ill Travelers
sources.notes: Fever is a measured temperature of 100.4 F (38 C) or higher. A measured temperature is the preferred method.

sources.title: FastStats: Sleep in Adults
sources.notes: Adults (18 and older) should get at least 7 hours of sleep each day.

sources.title: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) during spaceflight - a guideline for CPR in microgravity from the German Society of Aerospace Medicine (DGLRM) and the European Society of Aerospace Medicine Space Medicine Group (ESAM-SMG)
sources.publisher: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine (Hinkelbein et al., 2020)
sources.notes: Peer-reviewed guideline for CPR in microgravity (DOI 10.1186/s13049-020-00793-y). It gives no target compression rate or depth for microgravity.

sources.title: Hazard: Distance From Earth
sources.notes: Mars missions face a communication delay of up to 20 minutes one way.

sources.title: Speaking Percy's Language: How to Talk So Perseverance Will Listen
sources.notes: Commands take 3 to 22 minutes to reach the Perseverance rover on Mars, depending on planetary orbits.

sources.title: Ten things you didn't know about the Moon - Moon calling Earth
sources.notes: A signal takes on average 1.27 seconds to travel from the Moon to Earth.

sources.title: 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight
sources.notes: The five hazards of human spaceflight: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields (and the lack of gravity), and hostile or closed environments. The hazards can feed off one another.

sources.title: Risks of Human Spaceflight
sources.notes: Specific health risks linked to the five hazards. Weightlessness alters blood circulation and how the heart and blood vessels function. Isolation, radiation, distance from Earth and other stressors may take a toll on crew mental health. Also covers immune changes, bone loss, sleep loss and irregular schedules, nutrition, SANS (eye and brain changes), hypoxia and decompression sickness.

sources.title: Ongoing HRP Research
sources.notes: Current human research studies, e.g. Artemis II monitoring of well-being, activity and sleep (ARCHeR), Standard Measures (a consistent set of physiological and psychological measurements) and Tempus Pro (a telemedicine device for remote, near real-time diagnoses).

sources.title: Monitoring radiation for astronaut health
sources.license: Crown copyright (Government of Canada); see the site's terms and conditions
sources.notes: Radiation is a key challenge beyond Earth's atmosphere. Neutron radiation contributes about 30% of total radiation on the ISS; the CANS instrument measures neutron exposure continuously and autonomously.

sources.title: Why do we conduct science experiments in space?
sources.license: Crown copyright (Government of Canada); see the site's terms and conditions
sources.notes: The ISS is an orbiting laboratory. Moon and Mars missions mean more weightlessness, more radiation, longer isolation, longer communication delays with Earth, and less ability to rely on Earth for emergency medical assistance.

sources.title: NASA Open Science Data Repository
sources.notes: Real space biology datasets, to inspire and test the app. URL not yet verified.

sources.title: Heart palpitations
sources.publisher: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine) / A.D.A.M. Medical Encyclopedia
sources.license: Copyrighted (A.D.A.M. Medical Encyclopedia via MedlinePlus); linking allowed, own paraphrase only
sources.notes: A heart rate over 100 bpm is called tachycardia; lists when to seek emergency or prompt care.

sources.title: Slow heart rate - bradycardia
sources.publisher: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine) / A.D.A.M. Medical Encyclopedia
sources.license: Copyrighted (A.D.A.M. Medical Encyclopedia via MedlinePlus); linking allowed, own paraphrase only
sources.notes: Bradycardia is a heart rate below 60 bpm; it can be normal in athletes and during sleep.

sources.title: Measuring Your Blood Pressure
sources.notes: How to take an accurate home blood pressure reading.

sources.title: Blood pressure test
sources.license: Crown copyright; see NHS website terms
sources.notes: Home monitoring is usually done morning and evening; home readings of 135/85 or higher are usually considered high.

sources.title: Body temperature norms
sources.publisher: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine) / A.D.A.M. Medical Encyclopedia
sources.license: Copyrighted (A.D.A.M. Medical Encyclopedia via MedlinePlus); linking allowed, own paraphrase only
sources.notes: Normal body temperature ranges from about 36.1 to 37.2 °C; the accepted average is 37 °C.

sources.title: Temperature measurement
sources.publisher: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine) / A.D.A.M. Medical Encyclopedia
sources.license: Copyrighted (A.D.A.M. Medical Encyclopedia via MedlinePlus); linking allowed, own paraphrase only
sources.notes: How to take an oral or armpit temperature and how readings differ by site.

sources.title: Fever
sources.publisher: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine) / A.D.A.M. Medical Encyclopedia
sources.license: Copyrighted (A.D.A.M. Medical Encyclopedia via MedlinePlus); linking allowed, own paraphrase only
sources.notes: Home care for fever and when to contact a professional or get emergency help.

sources.title: Hypothermia
sources.publisher: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine) / A.D.A.M. Medical Encyclopedia
sources.license: Copyrighted (A.D.A.M. Medical Encyclopedia via MedlinePlus); linking allowed, own paraphrase only
sources.notes: Hypothermia is a body temperature below 35 °C and needs emergency help.

sources.title: Cardiovascular and Vision Laboratory
sources.notes: In weightlessness about 2 L of fluid shifts toward the head; orthostatic intolerance after flight.

sources.title: Spaceflight Standard Measures: Characterizing How Humans Adapt in Space
sources.notes: Crews do sensorimotor tests with heart rate and blood pressure before and after missions, plus sleep and mood questionnaires and actigraphy.

sources.title: Diabetes Testing
sources.notes: Fasting blood sugar of 99 mg/dL or below is normal; 100–125 prediabetes; 126 or above diabetes.

sources.title: Blood sugar test
sources.publisher: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine) / A.D.A.M. Medical Encyclopedia
sources.license: Copyrighted (A.D.A.M. Medical Encyclopedia via MedlinePlus); linking allowed, own paraphrase only
sources.notes: A fasting level of 70–99 mg/dL is normal; a lab test from a vein is more accurate than a fingerstick.

sources.title: Monitoring Your Blood Sugar
sources.notes: Step-by-step use of a blood sugar meter, written for people with diabetes.

sources.title: Diabetic Ketoacidosis
sources.notes: For people with diabetes: emergency signs including blood sugar that stays at 300 mg/dL or above.

sources.title: Symptoms & Causes of Diabetes
sources.notes: Common symptoms of diabetes; many people with type 2 diabetes have none.

sources.title: Screening for Prediabetes and Type 2 Diabetes
sources.notes: Clinical screening for adults 35–70 with overweight or obesity; every 3 years may be reasonable.

sources.title: About Sleep
sources.notes: Sleep needs by age, healthy sleep habits and keeping a sleep diary.

sources.title: Recommended Amount of Sleep for a Healthy Adult (AASM/SRS joint consensus, Watson et al., SLEEP 2015)
sources.license: © 2015 Associated Professional Sleep Societies; cite and paraphrase only
sources.notes: Adults should regularly sleep 7 or more hours; less is linked to adverse health outcomes.

sources.title: Sleeping in space
sources.license: Crown copyright (Government of Canada); see the site's terms and conditions
sources.notes: Astronauts are allotted about 8.5 hours for sleep each day.

sources.title: Prevalence of sleep deficiency and hypnotic use among astronauts (Barger et al., Lancet Neurology 2014)
sources.notes: ISS crew averaged about 6.1 hours of sleep per night by actigraphy; 75% of responding ISS crew used sleep medication.

sources.title: Risk from Inadequate Sleep and Irregular Schedules
sources.notes: ISS crews see 16 sunrises a day; LED lighting and scheduled rest are countermeasures.

sources.title: Patient Health Questionnaire-2 (PHQ-2)
sources.license: © 2026 National HIV Curriculum (page); instrument free to reproduce (see ctn_phq2)
sources.notes: PHQ-2 items and scoring; a score of 3 or more is the usual screening cut-off.

sources.title: NIDA CTN – Patient Health Questionnaire-2 (PHQ-2)
sources.publisher: NIDA Clinical Trials Network Dissemination Library
sources.license: Instrument: no permission required to reproduce, translate, display or distribute
sources.notes: PHQ-2 developed by Spitzer, Williams, Kroenke and colleagues; positive screens are followed up with the PHQ-9.

sources.title: Screening for Depression and Suicide Risk in Adults
sources.notes: No evidence on the optimal frequency of depression screening.

sources.title: Depression
sources.notes: In the U.S., call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline); in life-threatening situations call 911.

sources.title: Adult basic life support guidelines (2025)
sources.license: © Resuscitation Council UK; reproduction requires permission — paraphrase and link only
sources.notes: Unresponsive with abnormal breathing means cardiac arrest; on Earth, compress 100–120/min, 5–6 cm deep.

sources.title: CPR - adult and child after onset of puberty
sources.publisher: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine) / A.D.A.M. Medical Encyclopedia
sources.license: Copyrighted (A.D.A.M. Medical Encyclopedia via MedlinePlus); linking allowed, own paraphrase only
sources.notes: Check responsiveness, shout for help, 100–120 compressions per minute.

sources.title: Heart Attack - Symptoms
sources.notes: Heart attack warning signs; get emergency care even if you are not sure.

sources.title: Heart attack
sources.publisher: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine) / A.D.A.M. Medical Encyclopedia
sources.license: Copyrighted (A.D.A.M. Medical Encyclopedia via MedlinePlus); linking allowed, own paraphrase only
sources.notes: Rest may not relieve heart-attack pain; some people have little or no chest pain.

sources.title: Evidence Supporting the Management of Medical Conditions During Long-Duration Spaceflight: Protocol for a Scoping Review (Tran et al., 2021)
sources.notes: Acute coronary syndrome is first among 10 conditions prioritized for long-duration missions.

sources.title: Best Practices in End of Life and Palliative Care in the Emergency Department (Prachanukool et al., Clin Geriatr Med 2023)
sources.publisher: Clinics in Geriatric Medicine / PMC (author manuscript)
sources.license: PMC author manuscript, no CC license; cite and paraphrase only
sources.notes: Table 4 outlines OPQRST questions for a focused pain assessment (adapted from EMS1).

sources.title: Pain is vital in resuscitation in trauma (Saranteas et al., SICOT-J 2019)
sources.notes: Defines OPQRST (Onset, Provocation/palliation, Quality, Region/radiation, Severity, Time) for acute pain.

sources.title: Association Between Symptom Characteristics, Knowledge Sources, and Patient Interpretation of Acute Coronary Syndrome (Uchida et al., Circ Rep 2026)
sources.notes: A chest-pain registry evaluated symptoms with the OPQRST method.

sources.title: The incorporation of focused history in checklist for early recognition and treatment of acute illness and injury (Jayaprakash et al., BMC Emerg Med 2016)
sources.notes: ATLS and PALS recommend the SAMPLE acronym for a focused history.

sources.title: WHO-ICRC Basic Emergency Care: approach to the acutely ill and injured — Quick Cards (2018)
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO (per publication page https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241513081); item names and short paraphrase only
sources.notes: Lists SAMPLE history items and an SBAR handover format; diagnostic columns are not used.

sources.title: SBAR Tool: Situation-Background-Assessment-Recommendation
sources.license: © IHI, All Rights Reserved; cite and paraphrase only
sources.notes: SBAR is a structured way to frame a message that needs a clinician's attention.

sources.title: The Ship Captain's Medical Guide, 22nd ed., Chapter 13: External assistance (withdrawn edition)
sources.license: Open Government Licence v3.0 (gov.uk page); © Crown copyright
sources.notes: Historical maritime checklist of information to prepare before requesting radio medical advice; edition withdrawn in 2019.

sources.title: MGN 623 (M+F) Amendment 1: Telemedical advice service (TMAS) for ships at sea
sources.notes: The ship medical guide includes a form for TMAS information; photographs can help.

sources.title: Maritime telemedicine – state of the art. Consensus (IMHA/NCMM workshop, Malta, 2013)
sources.license: No license stated; cite and paraphrase only
sources.notes: Consensus calls for a pre-call form to assemble data on board before contacting telemedical services.

sources.title: Enabling Human Space Exploration Missions Through Progressively Earth Independent Medical Operations (EIMO) (Levin et al., IEEE OJEMB 2023)
sources.publisher: IEEE Open Journal of Engineering in Medicine and Biology / PMC
sources.notes: Two-way delay for Mars may reach 40 minutes; ISS medical data go to ground flight surgeons.

sources.title: Crew Autonomy During Simulated Medical Event Management on Long Duration Space Exploration Missions (Yule et al., Hum Factors 2023)
sources.license: CC BY-NC 4.0; cite and paraphrase only
sources.notes: Real-time consults may be impractical on Mars missions; checklists and guidance tools can mitigate delay.

sources.title: International Space Station Medical Operations (Jones, 2008 preprint)
sources.license: Work of the U.S. Government; public use permitted
sources.notes: ISS crews hold private medical conferences regularly and on request (2008).

sources.title: Communication delay increases procedure time and instructor task load during simulated suturing by novices (Yeam et al., npj Microgravity 2026)
sources.notes: In a small simulation (n = 8), a 4-second delay lengthened a remotely guided procedure.

sources.title: Development and Initial Validation of the PEG, a Three-item Scale Assessing Pain Intensity and Interference (Krebs et al., J Gen Intern Med 2009)
sources.publisher: Journal of General Internal Medicine / PMC
sources.license: © The Author(s) 2009; BPI items used with permission; cite and paraphrase only
sources.notes: 0–10 pain ratings are a format familiar to patients and clinicians.

sources.title: The utility and validity of pain intensity rating scales for use in developing countries (Pathak et al., Pain Rep 2018)
sources.notes: The 0–10 NRS (0 no pain, 10 maximum pain) gives enough options for precise ratings.

sources.title: Prehospital assessment of patients with abdominal pain triaged to self-care at home: an observation study (Larsson et al., BMC Emerg Med 2022)
sources.notes: Ambulance records of abdominal pain often missed history items such as last oral intake (11%).

sources.title: Cardiovascular and Cerebrovascular Control on Return from the International Space Station (CCISS)
sources.license: Crown copyright (Government of Canada); see the site's terms and conditions
sources.notes: Study of six astronauts. Devices recorded blood pressure, heart rate and physical activity over 24-hour periods before, during and after their missions, and the data from the ISS were compared with data collected before and after flight. It found significant differences between individuals, for example in how heart rate responded to changes in blood pressure.
